title: Water Transport and Transpiration Review Test
description: Connect roots, xylem, and leaves to water movement and evaluate evidence about plant water loss.

questions.prompt: Which pathway connects a wet root zone to water vapor in the air?
questions.questionText: Which pathway connects a wet root zone to water vapor in the air?
options: Roots -> sunlight -> air.
Roots -> xylem -> leaves -> air.
Leaves -> soil minerals -> sunlight.
Air -> roots -> dry rock.
questions.explanation: The pathway links uptake, transport, and loss from leaves.

questions.prompt: Why might a broad-leaved plant lose more total water than a smaller one without having a greater rate per unit area?
questions.questionText: Why might a broad-leaved plant lose more total water than a smaller one without having a greater rate per unit area?
options: Its leaves must contain no stomata.
A larger plant always loses less per area.
It has more leaf surface contributing to total loss.
Water loss is unrelated to leaf area.
questions.correctAnswer: It has more leaf surface contributing to total loss.
questions.explanation: Total amount and area-normalized rate answer different questions.

questions.prompt: A plant setup loses 18 g in six hours. What is the average rate?
questions.questionText: A plant setup loses 18 g in six hours. What is the average rate?
options: 3 g per hour.
6 g per hour.
12 g per hour.
108 g per hour.

questions.prompt: A water-loss experiment leaves one pot's soil uncovered and covers the other. Why is a leaf-only comparison uncertain?
questions.questionText: A water-loss experiment leaves one pot's soil uncovered and covers the other. Why is a leaf-only comparison uncertain?
options: Covered soil cannot contain roots.
Uncovered soil has no water.
Leaves must be identical if pots match.
Soil evaporation differs between setups.
questions.explanation: Different soil evaporation can contribute to measured mass differences.

questions.prompt: A plant closes many stomata during a dry afternoon. What paired effect is plausible?
questions.questionText: A plant closes many stomata during a dry afternoon. What paired effect is plausible?
options: Less water-vapor loss and less carbon dioxide entry.
More water loss and unlimited carbon dioxide entry.
No change to any gas exchange.
Immediate production of extra minerals.
questions.correctAnswer: Less water-vapor loss and less carbon dioxide entry.
questions.explanation: The same pores participate in both water loss and gas exchange.

questions.prompt: Which observation supports transport without proving photosynthesis?
questions.questionText: Which observation supports transport without proving photosynthesis?
options: Sugar measurements rise in matched light-grown leaves.
Carbon dioxide is taken up by illuminated green leaves.
Dye travels upward through a cut leafy stem.
Light energy is stored in newly formed sugar.
questions.correctAnswer: Dye travels upward through a cut leafy stem.
questions.explanation: Dye traces liquid movement; it is not evidence of sugar manufacture.

questions.prompt: Leaf area is 200 square centimeters and loss is 20 g; another plant has 100 square centimeters and loses 15 g over equal times. Which loses more per unit area?
questions.questionText: Leaf area is 200 square centimeters and loss is 20 g; another plant has 100 square centimeters and loses 15 g over equal times. Which loses more per unit area?
options: The first plant because 20 exceeds 15.
Both because they contain leaves.
The second plant, at 0.15 versus 0.10 g per square centimeter.
The first plant, at 10 g per square centimeter.
questions.correctAnswer: The second plant, at 0.15 versus 0.10 g per square centimeter.

questions.prompt: What must be added to a model predicting water loss solely from wind speed?
questions.questionText: What must be added to a model predicting water loss solely from wind speed?
options: A rule that all species behave identically.
Humidity, water supply, and stomatal responses can also affect loss.
A guarantee that roots supply unlimited water.
An assumption that leaves cannot regulate exchange.
questions.correctAnswer: Humidity, water supply, and stomatal responses can also affect loss.
questions.explanation: Water loss results from interacting environmental and biological factors.

questions.prompt: A plant's leaves stay firm after watering. Which claim goes beyond this evidence?
questions.questionText: A plant's leaves stay firm after watering. Which claim goes beyond this evidence?
options: Leaf firmness increased after watering.
Water balance may have improved.
Further observation could check whether recovery persists.
Watering restored every damaged root and proved the plant is fully healthy.
questions.correctAnswer: Watering restored every damaged root and proved the plant is fully healthy.
questions.explanation: Firmness is one indicator, not proof that every structure or process is restored.

questions.prompt: Why can humid air slow transpiration under similar conditions?
questions.questionText: Why can humid air slow transpiration under similar conditions?
options: Humidity eliminates all plant water.
Humid air turns stomata into roots.
Humidity supplies all food directly.
The water-vapor difference between leaf air spaces and surrounding air can be smaller.
questions.correctAnswer: The water-vapor difference between leaf air spaces and surrounding air can be smaller.
questions.explanation: A smaller vapor gradient can reduce outward movement.

questions.prompt: An experiment records a 16 g loss, but 5 g of water was collected from drainage. How much loss remains after subtracting known drainage?
questions.questionText: An experiment records a 16 g loss, but 5 g of water was collected from drainage. How much loss remains after subtracting known drainage?
options: 11 g, which still may include other pathways.
21 g, all transpiration.
5 g, all photosynthesis.
16 g, since drainage has no mass.
questions.correctAnswer: 11 g, which still may include other pathways.
questions.explanation: 16 - 5 = 11; remaining loss is not automatically all transpiration.

questions.prompt: A model identifies xylem as the main sugar-distribution tissue. What correction is needed?
questions.questionText: A model identifies xylem as the main sugar-distribution tissue. What correction is needed?
options: Xylem carries only sunlight.
All transport occurs outside the stem.
Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals; sugar transport involves phloem.
Roots make every sugar before leaves receive light.
questions.correctAnswer: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals; sugar transport involves phloem.
questions.explanation: Different conducting tissues have different major transport roles.

questions.prompt: A dry leaf surface is enclosed in a bag and droplets later appear. What strengthens the water-loss interpretation?
questions.questionText: A dry leaf surface is enclosed in a bag and droplets later appear. What strengthens the water-loss interpretation?
options: Only the leaf bag is observed once.
A matched empty bag has much less condensation and other moisture sources are considered.
The bag color is changed halfway through.
The soil is also enclosed without accounting for its evaporation.
questions.correctAnswer: A matched empty bag has much less condensation and other moisture sources are considered.
questions.explanation: A suitable comparison helps distinguish leaf-associated moisture from background sources.

questions.prompt: Why is wilting compatible with living cells?
questions.questionText: Why is wilting compatible with living cells?
options: Wilting necessarily removes every cell membrane.
Cells can lose enough water pressure to reduce firmness without all dying.
A wilted plant contains only dead minerals.
Living cells cannot change water content.
questions.correctAnswer: Cells can lose enough water pressure to reduce firmness without all dying.
questions.explanation: Turgor changes can affect shape before irreversible injury occurs.

questions.prompt: How does transpiration connect a plant to the water cycle?
questions.questionText: How does transpiration connect a plant to the water cycle?
options: Water taken up from soil can return to air as vapor.
Water atoms disappear when leaves dry.
All absorbed water stays permanently in roots.
Plants create all atmospheric water from minerals.
questions.correctAnswer: Water taken up from soil can return to air as vapor.
questions.explanation: Plants provide a pathway for water transfer between soil and atmosphere.
